There’s a good chance you’ve heard of Tadich Grill, given that the restaurant is older than San Francisco itself. It’s existed in one form or another since 1849, when it opened under the name Coffee Stand. That was one year before the city of San Francisco was formally incorporated, and 118 years before the restaurant moved to its current location on California Street in the Financial District. Tadich has been doling out fresh seafood and mesquite-grilled slabs of meat to patrons through a lifespan that has included multiple earthquakes, two world wars, Prohibition and multiple pandemics. It’s not merely the oldest restaurant in San Francisco, but in all of California. An eternal landmark. I only needed to walk through its doors on an early evening this August to understand why.

entry.title: What Referees Really Think About Automated Officiating Coming To The NBA
entry.summary: Replay reviews suck. Video replay once held so much promise in team sports. We would never have to watch another perfect game get ruined, never have to experience the agony of a blown call ending our team’s season. Instead, we’ve mostly gotten tedious, largely illogical uses of replay. Goals are routinely called back in the NHL because a few inches of an attacking player’s skate crossed the blue line in an offside position, even if it happened a full minute before the puck went in the net; the use of VAR in the Premier League has been so disastrous that the phrase “well done boys, good process” resurfaces as a grim joke every time the replay officials make a mess of something; replay has somehow made the definition of a catch in football harder to agree on.

entry.title: Luka Doncic Is Pushing All The Right Buttons
entry.summary: The Los Angeles Lakers are 15 games into the post-LeBron era, and things couldn't really be going better. A 118-114 overtime victory over the Hornets Tuesday night improved their record to 13-2, best in the NBA, and provided another reminder that this team is a much more fearsome and liberated than it has been over the last few seasons. This game would have been an easy one for the Lakers to let slip. They were without secondary offensive engine Austin Reaves and defensive fulcrum Walker Kessler, and the Hornets, while quite bad, are the kind of team that can get one over on a better opponent through annoying persistence. The Hornets lead the league in three-point attempts per game, which is not a problem in the aggregate given that they are shooting 31 percent from deep as a team, but can be a problem on certain nights when their three-point shooting percentage creeps closer to league average. They just about got there on Tuesday, making 18 of an appalling 54 three-point attempts. They shot well enough to earn a 13-point lead going into the fourth quarter. The Lakers are persistent, too. Nobody more so than Luka Doncic, who is somehow finding fresh frontier in this hyper-optimized era of the NBA. This guy has been doing crazy stuff: He leads the league in points per game (38.8), field goal attempts per game (25.4), three-point attempts per game (13.5), and free-throw attempts per game (10.8). It is not news to say that Doncic is an offense unto himself who is capable of melting any opponent in front of him—we saw him become precisely that in Dallas before a couple of idiots traded him away—but this version of Doncic feels new. James's exit has granted Doncic complete centrality within the Lakers' offense, and both he and JJ Redick appear zealously committed to making great use of his new circumstances.

entry.title: Consider This Awful Potential Consequence Of An MLB Lockout
entry.summary: Last night, as I lay awake in bed, I had a terrible vision of the future. It is summer. Major League Baseball's owners, in their greed and myopia, have locked out the players and delayed the new season of baseball indefinitely. I am desperate and miserable. The long, empty winter without the beautiful game has gored me of my winsome spirit and ability to dream, and now winter has stretched into spring. In this downtrodden state, I am forced to consider watching Banana Ball. Banana Ball, the sugar-coated exhibition league popularized by the Savannah Bananas, just keeps growing. Their games drew millions of fans in 2026 as the league expanded to six teams and completed a 45-state tour. Their games were broadcast on ESPN, which also regularly covers the league on ESPN.com. Now imagine what might happen during a whole summer in which no real baseball was being played, and stadiums around the country were empty. A lockout would bring many bad consequences, among them an opportunity for Banana Ball to fill the void left by MLB. The sport will be theirs for the taking. We may wake up one day and find that we are living in upside-down land, where the only people playing baseball on ESPN are those who come to the plate in stilts.

entry.title: Chargers Achieve Bare Minimum Of Dignity
entry.summary: You can call the Los Angeles Chargers many things: hopeless, depressing to think about, an ideal candidate for contraction. This blog could end right here and no one would think it was strange. But after Monday night's 23-20 victory over the Baltimore Ravens, you cannot call the Chargers winless. Before the season began, Chargers-Ravens seemed decent on paper as a national broadcast: two mid-tier AFC teams that should have been in playoff contention in Week 10. Alas, there was a lot of football to be played between then and now. Significant injuries to quarterbacks Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley effectively wrapped up Baltimore's season a couple of weeks ago. Apparently, Joe Fagnano was not the answer. The promise of the Ravens' 4-1 start has fully evaporated, and the rest of the AFC North simply looks better than them. Their best hope is somehow being reassigned to the NFC South within the next month. As for the Chargers ... woof. They lost eight straight games and grew increasingly appalling each week. QB Justin Herbert regressed so hard that it left a crater. Head coach Jim Harbaugh began to spend a significant amount of his time either issuing votes of confidence to various parties, or lobbying for his continued employment, as well as that of his new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel, who has firmly established that he's only a few letters away from Mike McCoy. Earlier this month, Chargers tight end Charlie Kolar was informed that the team's offense had gone 37 straight drives without scoring a touchdown, and he was visibly distraught. When I wrote their Why Your Team Sucks entry this summer, I felt a little hesitation in dumping so much on what was an 11-win team last season, but it turns out I didn't dump nearly enough.

entry.title: Buster Posey Is Our New Hall Of Fame Debate Topic
entry.summary: As an objective standard, baseball's Hall of Fame season provides a better list of managers and executives than players this year, which surely provides some wintry comfort for people who favor polo shirts, sunglasses, and a phone pressed against an ear while making frowny faces. But "objective standard" and the Hall of Fame have always been estranged, as should probably be the case. The only actually indisputable term here is "hall," because the physical plant is indeed that. Everything else is based on personal taste, and you can't have personal taste without persons, and you can't have persons without accepting that their version of objectivity typically begins with them objecting to someone else's version of same. It's how family fights over the holidays were invented. But your issues with your dimwitted cousin grabbing the last anything on the table are not why we're here. Buster Posey is, and oddly enough, so are Brian Sabean and Bruce Bochy. This is a circumstantially skewed San Francisco Bay Area-centered Hall of Fame season, especially when you add Dusty Baker and Sandy Alderson, but it's far less of a stretch to imagine Sabean and Bochy in particular being voted in by the Contemporary Baseball Committee than any of the players by the general electorate—despite the fact that Sabean and Bochy may not get into the Hall without Posey.

entry.title: Oh No, The Phones
entry.summary: Mom’s phone number was 620. If a friend wanted to reach her on her family’s farm just outside the rural Missouri town of Alma (pop. 400, more or less), they had to buzz the operator at the Alma Telephone Company and ask for the Corders or say, “Give me 620, please.” The operator, who probably knew by heart which circuit the Corders were on, would ring line No. 6 with the prescribed sequence: two long rings, zero short rings. The phones in 10 or so households all along the party line would let loose, with the ring pattern signaling to the other farmsteads that the call was for the Corder household. But anyone who wanted to pick it up could—and sometimes did. “You could usually tell when somebody else was on the line,” Mom said. Most often that somebody was Grandma Dieckhoff, who lived one house down the line with her son’s family. The ever-present possibility of eavesdroppers disciplined Mom’s high school chatter—except when it supercharged it: “We sometimes exaggerated a little to give her something to talk about.” Mom remembers precisely when her parents finally got off the party line, much later than most of the U.S.: December 1972, her freshman year at the University of Missouri. Late-adopting Alma Telephone skipped over rotary phones altogether, heading straight to direct dial. Grandma and Grandpa called her up, marveling at the ability simply to punch in 10 numbers to reach her, and only her.

entry.title: Irreal: Ramírez’s Emacs Contributions
entry.summary:
huge fan of Journelly, which I use many times a day as my memo book. It has many other uses so take a look at the link if you’re interested in a note taking/journaling/private tweet/memo book application. I can’t recommend it enough.
Ramírez has, of course, done many other things, many or perhaps most, in the Emacs sphere. See his site for details. In a recent post he writes about making contributions to Emacs and getting them merged. Those of you who have been down that road know that it’s hard to get started. You have to navigate the GNU copyright assignment process, which seems needlessly baroque until you remember that all this is being run by volunteers.
You can follow the link to find out what his contributions are. They are all live in Emacs 31 so if you are up to date they are available to you now. The main takeaway for me was the satisfaction that Ramírez got from making those contributions. None of them were huge changes and merely scratched an itch that Ramírez had. If you have a small itch that you’ve scratched, you should consider sharing it with the community. You too can become part of Emacs’ long and influential history just as Hari Seldon’s successors in the Second Foundation contributed their own additions to Seldon’s Psychohistory.

entry.title: Irreal: EWW As The Default Buffer
entry.summary:
made EWW his default browswer. That means that whenever he clicks on a URL and certain other links, the link is opened in EWW or—for special links—in another application that runs in Emacs. The point is, all browser activity starts in Emacs, usually in EWW.
Of course, Emacs can’t handle every browsing task so Blais uses the & key in EWW to escape to a “normal” browser. Blais says that EWW suffices for 85–90 percent of his use cases. He has some functions to kick off Emacs apps for MP4, PDF, and other specialized links. Everything else goes to EWW. He’s added a couple of custom bindings for EWW functions he uses a lot but it’s mostly a normal EWW instance.
Blais’ experiment shows that it is possible to almost browse from within Emacs. Sites that rely on JavaScript in an essential way are not going to work of course, and there are still a lot sites that insist on JavaScript so they can enforce the delivery of ads or implement a pay wall. Blais’ method gives us a chance to consider if those sites are worth viewing.

entry.title: Irreal: Setting The Timezone In Emacs
entry.summary:
hint for those of you who travel and phone home with Emacs. Here’s the situation: you are travelling and log into your home server with SSH and emacsclient. It’s wonderful. Just like being at home except the date/time stamp is wrong. The time and date are whatever your home server thinks they are but you want them to be local time.
The answer is simple. You simply need to change the TZ (timezone) environment variable to reflect your current location. For example, if you’ve travelled to New York (in the US) you would set TZ to “America/New_York”. Emacs, of course, provides a command to do this: (setenv "TZ" "America/New_York").
The zone codes can be a bit opaque so Choi has added a command to the latest Casual suite to set the TZ variable complete with completion. Take a look at his post if you’re interested.

entry.title: Charles Choi: Setting the Timezone in Emacs
entry.summary:
Here’s the problem: You are traveling in a different time zone from the Emacs server instance you are accessing remotely via ssh + emacsclient. All clock calculations in that Emacs session are using the local timezone relative to where the server is located. But what you really want is emacsclient to use the current timezone you are in, so things like the mode line clock render accordingly. To adjust the timezone in an Emacs session, use the command setenv to set the environment variable TZ with a timezone defined in the zoneinfo database. This can be called from Elisp as shown below.
1
(setenv "TZ" "Asia/Seoul")
The latest v3.1.0 update of Casual adds the command casual-timezone-set-tz that provides a completion interface for selecting a timezone to pass to setenv.
1
M-x casual-timezone-set-tz RET
Note that setting TZ impacts the Emacs session globally; any other running behavior depending on a clock should be taken into account.

entry.title: Raymond Zeitler: Creating a Note While org-capture is Active Can Be Confusing
entry.summary:
org-capture and then create a note1 while the capture is active (as I'm doing now), you might be very surprised when you press C-c C-c to finish the note -- it vanishes! Don't Panic! In order to see the note, you'll need to press C-c C-c a second time to complete the capture. Then org-capture adds the item into the Org file, along with the note.
My preference in this situation is to write only the first phrase or sentence of the note. Then I issue the two presses of C-c C-c and complete the note at its destination. I do this not only to avoid the "scary missing note" scenario; I also worry about leaving work unsaved for any amount of time. The computers I grew up with were prone to crashing at inopportune times, so I adopted the motto, "Save Early; save often." An Org note is composed in the *Org Note* buffer, which has no file associated with it and therefore is not a good candidate for saving. 1 With C-c C-z (org-add-note)

entry.title: Irreal: Journelly 1.5
entry.summary:
the release of Journelly 1.5. It’s the formal release of the beta version that I recently wrote about. I can’t say enough about this release. As I’ve said before, my Journelly database is over 4 thousand entries long and before this release Journelly was getting laggy and hard to use but this release resolved all those problems. Now Journelly is as snappy as it was when I had only a few entries and everything about it seems faster and easier.
But wait. There’s more. Ramírez has added an “on this day” feature as well as adding features that make searching for entries by date easier.
If you use Journelly as a journal, you may be interested in the new “on this day” feature. There’s a new button that will show you entries happening on the same day from other years. My particular use case for Journelly is as a memo book so I have no use for this feature. Fortunately, the new Journelly makes it easy to toggle it off if you don’t want it.
The other new significant feature is enhanced searching by date. In the search function you can use on: keyword with several different date formats to search for entries with a particular date. There’s also a calendar button that lets you choose the date from a calendar presentation if you prefer.
You may wonder why I have this entry tagged emacs. I consider Journelly intrinsically linked with Emacs because Journelly keeps its database in an Org file and that means that I can use Emacs and Org mode to search and edit that database. That doesn’t seem like much but I find myself doing it all the time. Journelly has become integrated into my Emacs workflow and become an important part of it.
In the mean time, those of you not in the Journelly beta program now have access to these updates. I can’t speak for Ramírez, of course, but if you’d like to be in the beta program, email Ramírez. He’ll probably be glad to add you.

entry.title: Charles Choi: Announcing Burnish
entry.summary: Org mode is often celebrated for its ability to “write once, export anywhere.” With such power comes added complexity: Exporting a file requires the user to typically go through a multi-step process (e.g. C-c C-e <some char> <some other char>). If the user is concerned with previewing changes to their file, then another step of viewing the exported output is required. Having to do this repeatedly gets tedious fast. Such is the motivation for Burnish. Burnish is a new Elisp package I’ve made to automate the export and viewing of an Org file. It provides an Emacs minor mode (burnish-mode) that when enabled, does the following upon save of an Org file: Export the Org file to a specified export backend. View the exported output in another Emacs window or by external tool. Most all of the default backends provided by Org mode are supported by Burnish. That said, Burnish is highly configurable, allowing for users to define for themselves the export and view workflow for existing or third party backends. Read the Burnish User Guide to learn more about it. As it is new, feedback is always welcome. If you really find it useful, please show your gratitude by buying me a coffee. Burnish v1.0 is now available on MELPA.

the Emacs 31.1.90 pretest is available. The Emacs point releases are generally to fix bugs and maybe refine an existing functionality but you shouldn’t expect any major new features. That will have to wait for Emacs 32. As always, the developers are asking for our help to test the release and let them know if we encounter any problems building or using it.
Be aware that there are some typos in Whitton’s post. In the first place, the pretest will eventually become Emacs 31.2 (not 31.1). More importantly, there are also typos in the URLs for the release. The correct URL is https://alpha.gnu.org/gnu/emacs/pretest/emacs-31.1.90.tar.xz and similarly for the signature file.
My usual thanks to the Emacs developers who work so hard for us and give us so much. As I always say, if one of us finds ourselves in the same bar as one of the devs, we’re buying.
